title: How Horseshoes Work
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explore horseshoes: the Springfield, Illinois horseshoe sandwich aside, the history of the horseshoe (from ancient horse booties to nailed iron shoes and the patron saint of farriers, St. Eligius), the game's ancient roots (Greek quoits, Roman and later American popularity), the National Horseshoe Pitchers Association, champion Alan Francis, court dimensions and stake setup, pitching techniques (single flip and one-and-a-quarter turn), and scoring under count-all and cancelation rules, plus house rules. The episode closes with a listener mail correction about Burning Man and a State Farm sponsor read.

segments.title: Opening banter and horseshoe sandwich
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter about a college backyard games course, lawn darts, and the Springfield, Illinois horseshoe sandwich, then discuss playing horseshoes with friends.

segments.title: History of the horseshoe
segments.summary: Horses were fitted with booties and sandals before metal horseshoes were nailed to hooves by about 1000 A.D. Nails are driven into the hoof wall, which has no nerve endings, and farriers do the work. St. Eligius is the patron saint of farriers.

segments.title: Ancient roots and spread of the game
segments.summary: Bent horseshoes were thrown like discuses, giving rise to quoits in ancient Greece. The game spread to America after the Revolutionary War and is played worldwide, with about fifteen million players in North America according to the National Horseshoe Pitchers Association.

segments.title: Alan Francis and the sport's top player
segments.summary: Alan Francis of Defiance, Ohio is described as the dominant champion, winning fourteen of the last seventeen men's World Championships and ringing about nine of ten throws. The hosts mention Josh Clark's book Perfection in the Horseshoe Pit.

segments.title: Rules, house rules, and game structure
segments.summary: Players pitch in pairs, throwing two shoes each in thirty seconds per inning, aiming to ring the stake. Games are commonly played to forty points, with house rules varying, such as win by two.

segments.title: Court dimensions and setup
segments.summary: A regulation court is forty-six feet long and six feet wide with two pitching platforms and iron stakes about thirty-six inches long set at a twelve-degree angle. Foul lines sit at twenty-seven and thirty-seven feet, with adult men pitching from thirty-seven feet.

segments.title: Horseshoe anatomy and pitching techniques
segments.summary: The parts of a horseshoe are the toe, heel, shanks, and calks. Two pitching methods are described: the single flip pitch, where the shoe may turn once or stay flat, and the one-and-a-quarter turn, where the shoe is held by the shank and turns to meet the stake.

segments.title: Scoring: count-all and cancelation
segments.summary: Count-all scoring gives three points for a ringer, two for a stay-in or leaner, and one for a shoe within six inches of the stake. Cancelation scoring cancels matching ringers, and only the closer shoe scores. The hosts joke about the scoring rules.

segments.title: Burning Man listener correction
segments.summary: A former Burning Man attendee writes to correct the hosts' episode on Burning Man, saying drugs and sex are a big part of the event, police are present, and there were DJ and musician sightings such as Paul Oakenfold and Perry Farrell.

segments.title: Sign-off and sponsor read
segments.summary: The hosts invite listener corrections through social media, email, and the website, then a State Farm sponsor message closes the episode.
